summary: Clarifies the Domain Naming Convention for Internet user applications and explores what adopting it means for internet name service and user applications. It is explanatory rather than a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains how the Internet came to use names built in layers, such as a host inside a site inside a top-level domain, instead of one flat host name. It describes the rules for those names, the servers that turn them into addresses, and the offices that hand them out.

questions: how do domain names resolve to addresses
subtitle: How names were built into a hierarchy of domains, and what that meant for name service and applications.

tldr.problem: The old ARPANET name Fred@ISIF only worked inside one network, so it could not name a host that was reached through another network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo replaces the single host name with a domain name built from simple names, running from the most specific on the left to the naming universe on the right, and gives each domain its own naming authority and name service.
tldr.outcome: RFC 819 is an explanatory memo, not a protocol specification. It has an Unknown status and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

today: RFC 819 is an explanatory memo with an Unknown status, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It sets out the hierarchical domain naming convention that the Internet community adopted and, as the memo says of itself, is a description of that convention rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: From Host Names to Domain Names
sections.content:
For many years the naming convention <user>@<host> served the ARPANET user community for its mail system, and the substring <host> was used for other applications such as file transfer and terminal access. With the advent of network interconnection, that convention had to be generalized to accommodate internetworking. A decision had recently been reached to replace the simple name field, <host>, with a composite name field, <domain>.

The memo shows the change in one line: the ARPANET convention wrote Fred@ISIF, and the Internet convention writes Fred@F.ISI.ARPA. The intent is that Internet names form a tree-structured hierarchy that depends on administration rather than on topology. The name components run from the most specific on the left to the most general on the right, so the root of the tree, the administrative universe, sits on the right.

The name service that realises the convention is assumed to be application independent. It is not part of any one application; a single independent name service serves several user applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier names said only which computer to use. The new names say which organisation, which site and which computer, so that the same name still makes sense when the computer sits on a different network.

sections.title: The In-Tree Model of Domains
sections.content:
The convention is built on the domain concept. The name of a domain is a concatenation of one or more simple names, and a domain is a region of jurisdiction for name assignment and for responsibility for translating names into addresses. The set of domains forms a hierarchy.

The memo models that hierarchy as a directed graph in which each node is a domain. An ordered pair (B, A), an arc from B to A, says that B is a subdomain of A and that B is a simple name unique within A. The graph that best describes the naming hierarchy is called an in-tree, a rooted tree with all arcs directed towards the root. The root represents the naming universe, the ancestor of all domains, and the endpoints or leaves of the tree are the lowest-level domains.

Uniqueness follows from the tree. A simple name is unique within its parent domain, and because the parent's simple name is unique within the grandparent domain, the concatenation of the two is unique in the grandparent domain, and so on up to the naming universe. Each domain has its own naming authority and its own name server, which is what lets the authority and the name service be spread out over the tree. Inside an endpoint domain, unique names are assigned to <user> to identify user mailboxes, and those mailboxes can be seen as children of their domain.

The memo admits that the model can be broken. Overlapping domains imply multiple parentage, meaning that an entity is a child of more than one domain. It is conceivable that ISI can be a member of the ARPA domain as well as a member of the USC domain, and the common child and the subtree below it then become descendants of both parents. The general implications of multiple parentage are left as a subject for further investigation.
sections.plainLanguage: Domains form a tree. Each one has a short name that is unique inside its parent, so joining the names of a domain and its parents gives a name that is unique in the whole tree. Each domain also has its own office that hands out names and its own server that answers questions about them.

sections.title: Absolute Names and the Trouble with Relative Ones
sections.content:
Absolute naming means that complete names are assigned with respect to a universal reference point, and the advantage is that such a name can be interpreted everywhere relative to that point. The Internet naming convention provides absolute naming with the naming universe as its reference point.

Relative naming is the alternative: an entity is named according to where the naming entity sits in relation to the named entity. A set of hosts running the unix operating system exchange mail using a method called uucp, and its convention is an example of relative naming. The recipient is named by a source route identifying a chain of locally known hosts that link the sender's host to the recipient's, so a destination name can be alpha!beta!gamma!john, where alpha is presumably known to the originating host and beta is known to alpha.

The uucp mail system shows the problems that relative naming creates. When host names are only locally interpretable, routing optimisation becomes impossible, and a reply may have to traverse the reverse route to the original sender in order to be forwarded to other parties. Worse, if a message is forwarded by one of the original recipients or passed on as the text of another message, the frame of reference of the relative source route can be completely lost.
sections.plainLanguage: An absolute name means the same thing to everyone, because it is measured from one fixed point. A relative name only means something to the machine that wrote it, and it stops making sense as soon as the message is forwarded elsewhere.

sections.title: Other Naming Conventions as Domains
sections.content:
To allow operation with a different naming convention, the names assigned by a foreign convention have to be accommodated. Because domains are autonomous, a foreign naming environment can be incorporated as a domain anywhere in the hierarchy, and the name service for a domain is provided within that domain. The result is that no standard convention for naming needs to be imposed in order to let different naming environments work together.

The memo gives two examples. There might be a convention in the FOO world of the form <user>%<host>%<area>, and a name from that world would be reached from the Internet community simply by appending .FOO, as in John%ISI-Tops20-7%California.FOO. One way of accommodating the uucp world is to declare it a foreign system, so that alpha!beta!gamma!john is known in the Internet community as alpha!beta!gamma!john.UUCP. A domain whose internal naming is complicated, and which the outside world neither knows nor cares about, is treated in the same way.

Mail makes the problem sharper, because the names written inside the message text are often used by the destination to reply. The embedded names may need to be converted for the benefit of the name server in the destination environment, and conversion of names on the boundary between two naming environments is a complex subject. The memo suggests viewing naming as a separate layer of protocol and treating conversion as a protocol translation. Appendix D lists the open questions, including what happens when a message goes to several destinations in different environments and when the destination does not share a boundary with the origin.

Mail relaying is the mechanism that makes such a boundary work. A relay is a point where a message is routed between the sender and the recipient, and the relay points are normally named explicitly in the delivery instructions, with each intermediate relay taking responsibility for the message. Relaying with absolute naming is a form of source routing in which every name, including those of the intermediate points, is universally interpretable, unlike the relative names of the uucp convention.
sections.plainLanguage: Other networks can keep their own way of writing names. The Internet treats each such system as one more domain in the tree, and a gateway between them translates names as it forwards messages.

sections.title: The Name Service, Iterative and Recursive
sections.content:
Name service is a network service that provides name-to-address translation, and it can be done in several ways. In a simple networking environment a single central database holding the correspondence between names and addresses will do. That is how the old ARPANET host names worked, with a copy of the database in every host. As the number of networks and hosts grew, the size of the database, its update frequency and the work of spreading it around became unmanageable.

The hierarchical structure of the Internet naming convention supports decentralised naming authority and a distributed name service. It accommodates growth of the naming universe, allows an arbitrary number of hierarchical layers, and adding a new domain adds little complexity to an existing system. The name service at each domain is assumed to be provided by one or more name servers, and the memo describes two models. An iterative name server may answer in two ways: with a destination address, which satisfies the query, or with the address of another name server, in which case the query must be repeated against that server and so on until a destination address is obtained. A recursive name server gives only one kind of answer, a destination address, which puts an obligation on it to make the call to another name server itself when it cannot answer the query.

Looping can be avoided, since the names presented for translation can only be of finite concatenation, though care is needed with mechanisms such as a pointer to the next simple name. The memo expects some name servers to be recursive and not all of them, so the caller has to be prepared for either type.

The basic name service at each domain is the translation of simple names to addresses for all of its children. Requiring complete names for every lookup would be unreasonable in practice, so the memo proposes partial names, used in the context where their uniqueness is preserved. A partially qualified name is built by omitting the ancestors that the communicating parties have in common, and it has to be qualified further as soon as it leaves that context. To support this, the name service at each domain must be able to resolve simple names for all of its ancestors, including itself, and for their children.
sections.plainLanguage: A name server either hands back the address or tells the caller to try another server, and it does that for the names in its own part of the tree. Because each domain owns its own names, the work is spread out instead of sitting in one big database.

sections.title: Registrars, the First Domain and the Applications That Use Names
sections.content:
Associated with each domain there must be a naming authority that assigns simple names and makes sure they stay distinct. The memo notes that if partially qualified names are allowed inside a sub-domain, uniqueness within that sub-domain is not enough on its own, because the name could still be ambiguous with a name outside it.

Administratively, each domain has a single person or office called the registrar. The registrar of the naming universe specifies the set of top-level domains and designates a registrar for each of them, and the registrar of any given domain maintains the naming authority for that domain.

The initial set of top-level names includes ARPA, which represents the organisations involved in the Internet system through the authority of the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, and so covers the research and development hosts on the ARPANET and hosts on many other networks as well. The memo warns against a wrong reading of this: the top-level domain ARPA does not map one to one with the ARPANET, because domains are administrative and not topological. During the transition from the ARPANET convention, a host name may be used as the simple name for an endpoint domain, so that USC-ISIF becomes the Internet domain USC-ISIF.ARPA.

Applications are expected to reach the service through ordinary program interfaces. For user applications such as file transfer and terminal access, the remote host needs to be named, and a host can be treated as an endpoint domain to stay compatible with the older convention. The memo recommends that the standard facility for translating a host name into an address be extended to accept names of the Internet convention, so that programs get a consistent interface, and that this facility use every mechanism the host has, such as a local table or cache of recently checked names, or a name server reached over the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each domain has an office that hands out names and keeps them unique, and one office at the top decides which top-level domains exist. The first of them was ARPA, which covered the research networks funded by the United States agency DARPA.
